factors.desc: Favorable or neutral coverage across the meta's IP archetypes and color strategies. With an expanded 15-deck meta field, decks with fewer polarized matchups perform more reliably across tournament swiss rounds.
Efficient AP usage and energy curve optimization for early and mid-game board development. Includes the ability to deploy threats ahead of curve and maintain proactive pressure.
Maximum damage output potential through Impact, Double Attack, Damage 2, and high BP thresholds. Measures how decisively a deck can close games once its win condition is assembled.
Overall value and composition of triggers in the deck's life area, including Color triggers for resource generation, Active triggers for board impact, and Final triggers for last-resort defense.
Reliable access to key characters and combo pieces through draw, search, and filtering effects. Decks that consistently assemble their core strategy outperform those reliant on natural draws.
Energy and AP economy, hand size management, and long-term card advantage. Measures how efficiently a deck converts its resources into board presence and damage over the course of a game.
Decision tree depth, AP sequencing complexity, and the gap between average and optimal play lines. Decks that reward mastery with significantly higher win rates score well here.
Ability to recover from life damage pressure, board wipes, and resource deficit through trigger activations, defensive keywords, and comeback mechanics.
Adaptable game plans, multi-color tech options, and the ability to pivot between aggressive and defensive postures depending on game state and matchup.

Ability to interfere with the opponent's board state, hand, or game plan through removal, Snipe, retire effects, and denial of key setups. Increasingly relevant as combo-oriented IPs populate the meta.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this midrange Kenpachi list makes a moderate number of meaningful turn-by-turn choices around AP and energy-line sequencing, but its sequencing traps are limited and its weak triggers and low disruption mean fewer response-timing decisions than control-style decks. Its high-BP bodies win many battles on their own, so a pilot who makes the obvious plays keeps much of the deck's win rate, while misplays on early AP turns are costly against fast aggro-tempo opponents.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Bomb Devil is a Tier 1 aggro-tempo deck whose core plan is to curve cheap Denji and Reze bodies into a Raid finisher, so most turns have a fairly clear line with some real choices about AP spending, when to commit the Bomb Devils and whether to hold Boom. Its timing demands are moderate: sequencing mostly means deploying energy-line characters before Raid turns, with fewer response-window issues than control-style decks. The deck's strong curve and playsets mean a competent but not expert pilot still wins much of the time, while close races against tempo lists are decided by the pilot's read on AP and Raid targets.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Inuyasha midrange is a mid-band Union Arena deck: its turns involve real but mostly straightforward choices about which characters to play, when to pay AP and energy, and when to commit Tetsusaiga into battle, with few deep sequencing traps. Its low tempo and weak draw mean misplays around energy and AP lines or a hand missing its key Inuyasha cards are costly, though a core that is easy to find and four copies of its best threat let it win much of the time on its own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kagurabachi Purple Iori Samura is a low-curve aggro-tempo deck whose main job is to get reliable early drops and attack from turn two, so most turns offer one fairly obvious line and the pilot's real choices are raid timing and when to commit to a push. Its cheap, redundant curve makes a strong draw win on its own against slower decks, though misplaying raid chains or trading badly against stronger tempo lists costs games, and its matchup spread is clearly uneven.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this aggro-tempo deck plays a fairly linear curve of Saito characters into a Kenshin Raid, so the typical turn holds a few real choices (which AP to spend on the raid versus a follow-up play, and when to commit against a blocker) rather than a dense puzzle. Its main skill demands are matchup judgment, knowing when the first wave is being out-valued by midrange decks, and sequencing 2 to 3 AP turns, while the strong early curve lets a new pilot win many games with the obvious plays.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Union Arena Standard tournament decks, this aggro-tempo list makes a moderate number of per-turn choices around AP spending, attack timing and when to commit bodies, but its cheap, closed three-character core makes most turns fairly obvious. Errors are punished because the deck has little resilience and card advantage, so a stalled or mistimed attack can lose, while its fast curve lets a new pilot keep much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange list asks for a moderate number of real choices each turn: how to spread AP across the cheap Kafka and Reno bodies, when to commit a high-BP Kaiju, and whether to hold defensive events for combat. Its key cards are straightforward to sequence, so timing matters only at a few moments, and misplays are usually recoverable thanks to the deep Kafka redundancy. Its main difficulty lies in matchup-dependent planning, since the deck must read whether it is the defender against fast tempo decks or the one applying pressure. The strong defensive floor and cheap early bodies make it fairly forgiving to pilot, though it still rewards careful resource management.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Cinderella Yellow Midrange is a straightforward curve-out deck: most turns have a clear main-phase play to make, with a handful of real choices about which character to commit, when to attack, and how to spend AP and energy. Timing matters less than in response-heavy decks because cards are used in the Main Phase, though sequencing the Cinderella line can still matter. Its weaknesses against fast aggro and wide boards mean the right plan shifts somewhat by matchup, and a missed early play or poor attack decision can cost the game, but the consistent four-of core and Grave redundancy let a competent but imperfect pilot still win many games on card quality.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Ichigo rewards constant decisions about which Ichigo version to deploy, when to build the Raid chain, and whether to commit Raid fodder versus holding resources, so it sits well above a simple aggro list in Union Arena Standard. Its Raid sequencing and the 1-AP Player One start raise timing and error sensitivity, though its strong raw power and Raid tempo mean a competent but imperfect pilot still does reasonably well. Matchup variance is moderate, with the deck adjusting its pace against fast aggro versus slower midrange, and autopilot is middling because the high power ceiling is real but converting it depends on careful pilot choices.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Yellow Shin Asakura list asks for several real choices per turn around AP ramp, when to commit energy-line characters and which raids to make, but its core plan of cheap Heisuke bodies into high-BP Shin Asakura front liners is fairly direct. Sequencing and response-timing demands are moderate, matchup adjustments are modest since the deck is built to avoid polarized matchups, and a clumsy hand can stumble on ramp, so misplays are costly without being razor-thin. Its strong bodies win many games by themselves, so a competent new pilot keeps much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Royal Guard play asks for regular choices about when to pay the AP and energy line, which characters to play, and when to trade up in BP battles, but the core plan is fairly linear compared with the faster or more interactive Union Arena decks. Its slow AP ramp and lack of disruption make it punish poor sequencing against aggro, and it leans on strong draws and a readable board plan, so a competent pilot keeps much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, Aki Hayakawa Raid Midrange asks for several real choices each turn: sequencing the AP and energy line from a clunky 1 AP / 2 AP opening, deciding when to Raid and which base character to replace, and deciding when to hold Revenge! for removal. The Raid chain has ordering and sideline-versus-removal-area considerations, and misplays against wide or aggro-tempo boards are often punished, while the raid bodies and Makima give the deck enough power that a competent but not expert pilot still wins a fair share of games.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Raid sequencing and deciding when to set up the chain give this deck a meaningful number of choices each turn, above a simple aggro list. Its single-color build and cheap energy line keep the core plays obvious, and its lack of disruption means the pilot's main job is developing the board, so it sits near the middle of the competitive Standard field on difficulty.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Rimuru Raid Midrange asks for several meaningful choices each turn: when to fill the energy line with Soei and Gobta bodies, when to commit toward Raid targets, and which Rimuru to draw toward. Sequencing matters moderately, mainly around timing the raid and managing AP and energy. Its matchup plan shifts with the opponent's speed, and a slow start against aggro decks is punished, but the deck's raid power and filtering cushion many errors. Its cards carry it reasonably well, though converting the Raid line still needs skilled pilot decisions.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Production Model-02 Raid Aggro asks for a steady stream of attack and energy-line decisions each turn, mainly around when to raid into the Beast Form spike and which blockers to clear with the crossbow, but the core line is fairly direct. Its fragility in the face of boards that stall Raid and its dependence on drawing the right base character push the pilot toward matchup reads and mulligan judgment, while the cheap-body curve lets a competent but not expert pilot convert much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Green Saitama is a straightforward midrange deck: its curve of Genos, Silverfang and Suiryu fills the energy line quickly and its King engine gives repeatable setup, so most turns have one clear play. Its skill ceiling comes mainly from managing AP and sideline resources and from judging when to commit Saitama into blockers, while the low trigger value and lack of card draw mean a poor draw is hard to recover from.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange-control list asks for a moderate number of real choices per turn: when to commit characters to the energy line, which Natsuki Seba to deploy, and when to hold back. Its main skill demand is matchup management, since it loses to aggro and Raid lists and needs a different plan against slower decks. Its slow curve and lack of a finisher make mistakes somewhat forgiving, while the deck's main-character plan gives it fewer autopilot wins than a faster list.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Red Eren Midrange asks for many card-by-card choices each turn across the AP ramp, Raid targeting, and Basement sequencing, which puts it above a simple midrange list. Its Attack Titan forms and high BP let a reasonable pilot win without fine play, but the slow start and clunky draws mean a mistake in sequencing or tempo is often costly.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Yuji is a fast aggro-tempo deck whose turns involve real choices about AP and energy-line placement, with Black Flash and Domain Expansion adding burst decisions. Its low-cost base makes the early curve forgiving, but a misjudged race against faster or disruptive matchups and an empty hand are harder to recover from, and the pilot must read the matchup closely.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Rem Raid Tempo is a fairly linear aggro list: most turns follow an obvious curve of deploying Subaru bodies and Raiding Rem onto them, with a handful of real choices about which Raid to take and when to commit AP. Sequencing matters mainly in turn-one-to-three AP ramp, and misplays are recoverable against many slower decks, but a hand without early Subaru bodies is punished. Against larger midrange boards the plan shifts, giving moderate matchup variance, and the cards carry a lot of the win rate on their own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Raid Aggro is a fairly linear aggro deck: most turns are developing energy-line characters and attacking with Raid into the finishers, so per-turn decisions are moderate, mainly around which front-line target to remove and when to commit. Sequencing matters somewhat (keeping the Raid chain intact and reaching the 3 AP turn), but timing windows are simple, and the deck's power and curve let a new pilot win many games on the obvious plays. Errors are punished when the front line is lost or the chain stalls, but the deck's aggression usually absorbs small misplays.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena decks, this midrange Kisho Arima list asks for a moderate number of real decisions per turn: sequencing the energy-line starters against the AP curve and choosing when to commit Kisho Arima into the board. Timing and error punishment sit around the middle, since the deck has few trigger slots and little interaction on the opponent's turn, so fewer response windows exist to misjudge. Matchup variance is moderate because the deck's plan shifts between racing aggro and grinding midrange, while its deep Kisho Arima top end lets the cards do much of the work for a competent but not expert pilot.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena decks, this Byakuya Raid-line midrange has a moderate number of real decisions per turn, centered on when to commit characters to the energy line and when to set up the Raid turn, and it carries a noticeable skill ceiling from managing AP and Raid timing. The strong Byakuya density makes the obvious line easy to execute and gives the deck a high autopilot factor, though a misplayed sequence or a mistimed Raid can lose tempo against fast aggressive opponents.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Raid midrange deck asks the pilot to build the energy line, time Raid chains, and choose targets each turn, with a skill ceiling above the typical competitive deck. Misordering characters or overextending into Raid-stacked removal punishes errors, and the deck's aggro-facing weakness means matchup plans change meaningfully. Its power comes partly from the Mayuri and Nemu cards, so a new pilot keeps some win rate, but the close games are decided by sequencing and read quality.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena's typical competitive deck already involves regular resource and board decisions, and this midrange Shunsui deck adds a meaningful energy-line build decision alongside AP trade-offs between developing characters and using Events from turn three onward. Sequencing matters around the energy line and Aizen's mid-game timing, but it is less intricate than the most demanding decks, and its pilot can lean on a deep Shunsui pool for obvious early plays, so the cards carry a fair share of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this mono-red Arima Raid list makes a modest number of real decisions per turn: mostly which bodies to commit to the energy line and when to Raid with Kisho Arima onto a developed board. Its sequencing demands are light, but misjudging the Raid timing or ignoring fast aggro pressure can cost the game. Its cards do much of the work, since cheap bodies and a strong Arima swing turn let an average pilot win many games without expert reads.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Emilia is a midrange-tempo deck whose core 4-copy energy line and wide Emilia package give a fairly clear default play most turns, so it is simpler to pilot than the more intricate decks in Standard. Decisions center on front-line versus energy-line positioning and Raid timing, and the deck's power is spread across many Raid targets, so a competent but not expert pilot keeps much of its win rate. Misplays in the 1/2/3 AP ramp and against fast aggro decks are noticeably punished, which keeps error punishment in the moderate range.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Shion Raid Midrange asks for several meaningful decisions per turn: when to play energy-line characters versus raid cards, how to spend AP, and which character to raid with, and the 3-AP turn is a real timing bottleneck. Matchup variance is notable because the deck is slow against pressure decks like Sakamoto Days, and its lack of disruption makes its plan shift by opponent. Its raw card quality and consistent shape mean the obvious plays win many games, which keeps autopilot fairly high, while errors in raid sequencing and life management are punished moderately rather than severely.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Rimuru Midrange sits in the middle of a competitive Union Arena Standard field: it asks for several real decisions a turn around energy-line building, Raid timing and positioning, but its core Rimuru base and smoothing cards let a competent autopilot line play out reasonably. Its slow start against faster pressure makes matchup adjustment and sequencing moderately important, while errors are usually recoverable rather than immediately fatal.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this Purple midrange build has a moderate number of real decisions per turn: sequencing energy-line bodies, timing Arise, and deciding when to commit Sung Jinwoo threats against the opponent's board. Its skill ceiling is elevated by Raid-chain and name-target tracking across several Sung Jinwoo numbers, but its midrange shell and cheap early bodies let a pilot who simply curves out win a good share of games, so autopilot value is fairly high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Green Milim aggro is a straightforward plan: deploy the Ramiris and Milim base, attack with high-BP Milim variants, and make few hard choices per turn. Timing and sequencing matter little, and the four-copy redundancy of several Milim variants means the obvious line wins much of the time. The pilot still has to judge block/trade timing against faster aggro and value decks, and it has few adaptation tools, so matchup and error costs sit in the moderate range.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Purple Naraku asks for regular decisions around when to deploy the Raid base, how to fund the payoff against a tight AP ramp, and how to spend energy across the Main Phase, with the skill_ceiling of 52 and resource_management of 40 supporting a mid-high decision load. Sequencing matters because the Raid plan needs the base and payoff in the right order, and a stalled early turn is hard to recover from against fast aggro decks. The deck's plan shifts noticeably between aggressive and defensive matchups, but the core game plan stays recognizable, and its power comes partly from the Naraku cards, so a competent pilot keeps much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange Green deck is mid-to-low on difficulty: most turns have an obvious development line once the energy line runs, with the main decisions being when to commit characters to the energy line versus the front line and when to use Raid. Its slow ramp and thin defensive triggers mean misplays about tempo and sequencing are noticeably punished, but the cards' core is coherent enough that a new pilot keeps much of the deck's win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Sequencing matters somewhat through the early energy build, but there is little instant-speed response play to manage. The deck's cheap early characters and Raid payoff let a competent pilot win with straightforward play, so its autopilot factor is fairly high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Miroku/Sango midrange deck is a straightforward, mostly consistent list: its key cards and energy-line plays are fairly obvious, so turns hold a few real choices (when to deploy, which front-line exchange to take with Wind Tunnel or Hiraikotsu) rather than dense branching. Sequencing and response timing matter less than in more reactive decks, and a misplay is usually recoverable at the cost of tempo, though falling behind a fast starter and running out of finishers can decide close games. The deck's core cards carry much of the win rate on their own, which keeps the autopilot score high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Nano Eiai midrange is a straightforward curve-and-attack deck whose typical turns offer a few real choices about deployment and attacks, with only occasional sequencing decisions compared with more complex Union Arena lists. Its matchup-driven weakness to aggro and lack of disruption means plan adjustments matter somewhat, while mistakes are moderately punished by its slow start, but a predictable board and strong cards let a new pilot keep much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Annie is a mid-tier midrange deck whose main decisions revolve around when to spend AP on raids and upgrades versus developing the energy line, giving it moderate per-turn choices but few deep sequencing traps. skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Raid deck asks for several meaningful choices per turn: when to deploy low-cost bodies to fill the energy line, which base to Raid into which payoff, and how to pace the tempo curve against aggro. The Raid sequencing carries moderate timing stakes, while the matchup plan shifts between aggro pressure and the mid-game Raid turns. skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Zeke Jaeger is a single-color midrange deck whose main decisions are when to deploy the Zeke payoffs, which Zeke to play, and how to use Titan Injection, which gives it moderate decision density but little sequencing depth. Its plan is mostly straightforward once the energy line is online, so errors are only moderately punished, while the deck's raw card power lets a competent but unpolished pilot keep much of its win rate, and matchups shift mainly around facing fast aggro versus disruptive setups.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Yellow Titan Shifter Raid midrange deck asks for regular decisions each turn about which Raid target to use, when to switch characters to the front line, and when to hold energy for the Rumbling finish, but its core line is fairly direct. Sequencing matters at key moments such as Raid timing and mulligan decisions, while mistakes such as Raid cards stranded without a base or a slow opening are costly though often recoverable. The strong power ceiling and straightforward Raid plan let a competent draw win a lot on its own, so the pilot is important but the cards do much of the work.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Most turns involve a handful of real choices about what to deploy and what to hold, but the sequencing is rarely precise or punishing, and the deck's powerful threats do much of the work on a good draw. Its weaknesses against fast aggro and its lack of disruption mean matchup awareness and resource planning matter, keeping it moderately demanding relative to other Standard decks.

Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks it is moderate in difficulty, with the pilot mattering most in race and sideline-management decisions.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Hisoka is a midrange deck with a clear curve and reliable four-of core cards, so most turns offer a few meaningful choices about Raid upgrades, AP spending and energy-line timing rather than a dense web of decisions. The consistent core lets a fresh pilot keep much of the deck's win rate, but the skill ceiling is raised by Raid sequencing and the limited disruption.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Sukuna is a midrange deck with a clear early energy line and several recognizable plays per turn, so the decision load is moderate rather than extreme when compared with other competitive Standard decks. Its power comes mostly from strong top-end Sukuna threats and Sukuna's Finger setup, so a new pilot can reach a reasonable win rate by curving out, but the deck still asks for careful energy-color management, Yuji variant selection and matchup-aware pacing against fast aggro versus slower decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Beatrice is a competitive midrange-control shell with a fairly steady curve of four-of Beatrice and Subaru copies, so most turns make a clear energy-line and Raid decision rather than a dense branching puzzle. Sequencing and resource spending (AP and energy line timing) matter moderately, and a misplayed early turn can be punished by faster decks, but the deck's consistency and redundancy absorb many small errors. Relative to other Standard Union Arena decks it sits in the middle of the difficulty range, with the pilot's management of hands and matchup-specific pacing as the main skill test.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Rem is a midrange-tempo deck with a smooth, low curve, so each turn offers several real decisions around deploying characters and committing to Raid plays, but most turns still have an obvious line. Sequencing matters moderately, mainly around the Raid chain and when to hold resources, without the precise multi-step ordering seen in the most demanding Union Arena lists. Matchup variance is notable because the deck's role shifts against fast aggro versus grindier midrange, and the pilot must know which race to play. Misplays are fairly forgiving thanks to consistent energy and four-of density, though losing a close damage race can be decided by a single mistimed attack. The deck wins a fair amount from its cards on a good draw, so autopilot is above the midpoint.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this Red Kenshin Raid Midrange deck has a moderate number of real choices each turn, mainly around energy-line sequencing, when to Raid onto a deployed Kenshin, and which character to bring in. Its heavy four-copy redundancy and a fairly direct plan make it more forgiving and autopilot-friendly than the most intricate decks, though keeping the base Kenshin alive and managing red energy adds some punishment for misplays. Matchup adjustments against fast aggro decks are meaningful but not sweeping.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange Purple Shadow Army deck asks for real choices each turn: sequencing the energy line, deciding when to Raid Sung Jinwoo onto cheap bodies, and balancing board presence against holding resources. Its high skill ceiling and power ceiling reward careful Raid-timing and resource management, but its dense low-cost base and strong card quality let a competent but less precise pilot still win many games. Matchup play against fast aggro decks is meaningful but not as demanding as the most punishing lists in the format.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Kirito/Sinon is a straightforward aggro-tempo shell: most turns put out an obvious character and attack, with real decisions concentrated in battle targeting, Photon Sword use and when to hold energy for the top end. Errors are punished moderately because the deck folds quickly when behind and has weak life-area triggers, but its consistent 4-of curve and single-color base let a competent pilot win many games without heavy sequencing skill.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Tempo Evangelion decks in Union Arena rely on a dense low-cost curve and a repeatable top-end threat, so most turns are fairly clear developments with a few real choices about deploying versus holding and when to commit the Test Type-01 line. Their limited interaction and thin recovery mean misplays in racing or front-line trades are punished moderately, while the deck's raw card quality wins many games on its own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Chihiro Rokuhira deck has a straightforward plan with a few meaningful choices per turn: when to commit characters to the energy line and which attacks to make. Sequencing is simple, so timing sensitivity is low, while matchup variance is moderate because the deck's slow start is exposed against aggro decks. Its consistent bodies and mid-game threats let the cards do much of the work, giving it a high autopilot factor, and the lack of disruption and draw means misplays are only moderately punished.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Taro Sakamoto Raid-chain yellow is a tournament aggro-tempo deck with a clear default line: build the yellow energy line with Hana, Aoi or Lu, then Raid Taro each turn, so decisions centre on energy sequencing and when to commit into a board. Raid chains and sidelined underlying cards make errors costly, but the deck's power lets a fairly straightforward pilot win most games, and its plan shifts only moderately across matchups.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Purple Toguro is a midrange deck with several meaningful per-turn choices (which character to play, when to raid, how to spread AP and energy across the energy line), but the core curve is fairly linear and the sturdy Toguro bodies forgive mid-level misplays. Sequencing matters less than in deeper Union Arena builds, though the spread across many card numbers and raid timing add some awkwardness, and matchups against Purple Ichigo or Sung Jinwoo shift the plan meaningfully. Scores sit near the middle of the competitive Standard field, with lighter autopilot than a top-tier deck because the list is untested and its raid swings need correct sequencing to convert.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Asta aggro is a simple, consistent list that produces similar openings and wins largely on pressure, so decisions per turn and sequencing traps sit below the typical Union Arena tournament deck. Its main skill demands are deciding when to commit Demon-Slayer Sword, sequencing the energy line on turns 1-3, and reading when to race versus hold blockers, with misplays mattering moderately because the deck has little recovery after trading.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Envy is a midrange shell with a clear early curve of Envy energy-line bodies and a repeatable Lust/Father board, so most turns offer a few real choices (what to deploy, when to hold Bradley or Philosopher's Stone) rather than dense branching. Timing and error punishment sit mid-range because sequencing mostly concerns which Envy to play first and when to commit, with stalled hands the main way mistakes cost games, while the deck's stable board gives it a moderate autopilot floor.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Kikoru aggro-tempo deck makes a handful of real choices each turn around energy-line setup, the order of AP cards switched to resting, and when to commit Kikoru, but the early curve is fairly obvious. Its skill demand is moderate: sequencing and matchup reads matter against Sakamoto Days or Jujutsu Kaisen aggro, and a misplayed energy line or an awkward hand can cost the race, yet a competent aggressive pilot following the curve wins a good share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Asuna is a mid-difficulty midrange deck within the Union Arena Standard field: its energy-line-then-front-line structure gives a few real decisions per turn, mainly around sequencing AP and energy-line setup and when to commit Goddess characters. Its strong duplication of key characters makes the obvious play usually correct, so much of its win rate comes from the cards, while mulligans, awkward AP turns and a thin early curve do punish mistakes against fast decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Evangelion Mari Tempo is a relatively straightforward all-character curve deck: most turns follow an obvious ramp-and-deploy line, with real decisions around AP spending when events and expensive Asuka/Misato compete, and in matchups against blockers. Sequencing and timing matter modestly, and misplays are usually recoverable given the redundant playsets, though low resilience against aggro decks raises the cost of errors. Its cards carry much of its win rate, so a competent but not expert pilot keeps most of its results.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Sesshomaru Raid-Midrange deck sits in the middle of the competitive field: each turn asks real questions about Raid targets, energy-line sequencing and when to commit characters to positions, with a skill ceiling of 52 reflecting that depth. Its weak early curve and lack of draw or removal mean misplays in building the energy line or choosing Raid targets are costly, but the strong finisher cards (Bakusaiga, Sesshomaru variants) let a fair draw win without expert handling, which keeps the autopilot score moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Modernia midrange is a mid-tier, fairly straightforward deck: its cheap Marian and Rapi energy line and full playsets make most turns follow an obvious sequence, so autopilot play wins a fair share of games. Its pilot-dependent moments come from deciding when to commit Modernia and Red Hood, sequencing the energy line, and deciding how to handle fast Yellow aggro with little interaction. Compared with other competitive Union Arena decks it has limited ability to answer boards and few draw or search effects, which keeps its skill ceiling moderate rather than high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: As a single-color midrange-tempo deck built on a reliable early curve of Crusch Karsten, its turns offer a moderate number of real choices about deployment, attacks and holding a blocker, but most turns are fairly straightforward. Sequencing matters mainly around assembling the Crusch & Ferris Raid core and timing One Blow, A Hundred Felled, so the timing demands are modest. Because the deck leans on natural draws and has limited disruption and few Final triggers, a misplay in the mid-game is moderately costly, while its strong curve lets the cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Rurouni Kenshin Purple is a low-curve aggro-tempo deck whose main decisions are when to build the energy line, when to raid-upgrade a cheap body, and whether to attack into equal-BP blockers, so it sits in the middle of the Union Arena competitive field rather than at the complex end. Its skill ceiling is moderate: the obvious curve play wins a fair share of games, but losing the early race to faster decks or stalling on equal-BP blockers is hard to recover from, and matchup spread is low, so the same plan works in most games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Purple Sojiro Seta is a midrange deck with a consistent, easy-to-deploy key character and a straightforward Raid-based curve, so the obvious line wins a fair share of games. Real decisions arise around when to upgrade, when to develop and how to spend AP and energy, while sequencing and matchup adjustments matter moderately without being punishing. Its low disruption and weak trigger density keep the pilot's skill relevant in close games, but the cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Levi is a midrange deck with several real decisions each turn around which Levi variant to play, when to Raid onto Erwin or Petra, and how to spend AP and energy, but its core lines are fairly linear compared with the more complex Union Arena decks. Sequencing matters mainly around Raid timing and holding Levi's Barrage, and a slow start against aggro is a matchup issue more than a punishing error. The cards do much of the work by themselves, so a competent pilot who makes the obvious Raid plays wins a fair share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Asuna midrange, a Tier 4 list with mid-range factor scores, asks for a steady stream of front-line and energy-line placements each turn, with several meaningful choices about what to deploy and when to attack. Its low curve and four-of core make the obvious lines carry much of the win rate, while sequencing between the front and energy lines and the lack of reach or removal mean a skilled pilot separates itself in close games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive pool this Blue Ichigo midrange deck asks for a steady stream of Main Phase choices about energy line setup, AP spend between Raid and Bankai, and when to commit Raid targets, which pushes decision density moderately above the simpler decks. Timing sensitivity is lower because the deck's sequencing is mostly a matter of establishing the energy line before attacking, with few response-window traps. The deck's four-copy Ichigo playsets and Zangetsu/Bankai pressure let a straightforward curve win many games, so autopilot is fairly high, while a slow Player One start and tight 3 AP budget keep error punishment and matchup adjustment meaningful.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rukia Freeze Midrange asks the pilot to choose between building the energy line, assembling Raid steps, and holding freeze/rest effects, which gives a moderate number of real decisions per turn. Its sequencing matters for when Raid is triggered and when resting or freezing is applied, but it is less timing-critical than the most combo-heavy competitive decks. Matchup adjustments are significant against fast tempo decks versus grindy ones, while the near-duplicate Rukia copies and simple board-building lines keep the autopilot level fairly high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Raid-based Solo Leveling shell with a consistent, full-set setup; each turn has several meaningful choices around energy line, AP spend and when to commit Raids, but sequencing is not especially precise. The deck's card quality does much of the work for a competent pilot, with decisions mainly about matchup handling against fast Aggro-Tempo decks, so it sits in the middle of the competitive Standard field.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Edward Elric list has a consistent, repetitive core plan with few sequencing traps and little reactive timing on the opponent's turn, so it is comparatively forgiving and easy to pilot. Its main skill demands are judging when to race versus stabilize against faster Aggro-Tempo decks and managing energy and draw redundancy, which lift it modestly above the simplest decks.

cardMetrics.desc: How many different decks or IP archetypes the card fits into, distinguishing cross-IP staples from IP-specific role-players.

cardMetrics.name: Power Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card improves win rate when drawn or played, measuring its direct contribution to winning game states.

cardMetrics.name: Consistency Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card contributes to reliable execution of the deck's core game plan through search, draw, or filtering.

cardMetrics.name: Meta Relevance
cardMetrics.desc: Current competitive usage rate and frequency across top tournament placements and winning decklists.

cardMetrics.name: Replaceability
cardMetrics.desc: How easily the card can be substituted without meaningful loss in deck quality; lower replaceability indicates higher importance.

cardMetrics.name: Synergy Value
cardMetrics.desc: How well the card enables or benefits from interactions with other cards in its archetype, measuring combo potential and IP-internal cohesion.
